Fury
fū´rĭ
n. (violent anger; rage; rendering Hebrew chemah, Greek thumos)
From Latin furor, rage or madness. Scripture is careful with the word: God's fury is settled judicial heat against sin, never the loss of self-possession, and the fury of men is exactly that loss.

Biblical Definition

Fury renders a Hebrew word for burning heat, and Scripture applies it to God and to men in ways that must be kept distinct. In God it is judicial, announced beforehand, and avoidable by repentance: “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart… lest my fury come forth like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings” (Jeremiah 4:4). The fury is conditional upon impenitence and is preceded by a call to circumcise the heart. It is also purposeful rather than uncontrolled: “I will cause my fury to rest upon them… and they shall know that I the LORD have spoken it in my zeal” (Ezekiel 5:13). And it can be truly denied of Him toward His own vineyard: “Fury is not in me: who would set the briers and thorns against me in battle?” (Isaiah 27:4). In men the same word describes the collapse of self-command, and Scripture gives it a face: “Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury, and the form of his visage was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: therefore he spake, and commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated” (Daniel 3:19). Fury altered his countenance and made him foolish, since a furnace seven times hotter did not touch the three men at all.

Webster 1828 Definition

Rage; violent anger; madness; turbulence. Scripture distinguishes the LORD's fury — judicial, declared beforehand, and turned aside by repentance — from the fury of men, which disfigures the face and unseats the reason.

expand to see more

FURY, n. [L. furia, from furo, to rage.] A storm of anger; madness; rage; a violent passion of the mind.

2. Enthusiasm; heat of the mind; as, poetic fury.

3. Violence; impetuous motion; as, the fury of the winds or of a tempest.

4. In mythology, a deity represented as an avenging spirit; hence, a turbulent, violent woman.

FURIOUS, a. Rushing with impetuosity; violent; raging; mad; transported with passion.

FURIOUSLY, adv. With impetuous motion or agitation; violently; vehemently.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 4:4 — "Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: lest my fury come forth like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings."

Ezekiel 5:13 — "Thus shall mine anger be accomplished, and I will cause my fury to rest upon them, and I will be comforted: and they shall know that I the LORD have spoken it in my zeal, when I have accomplished my fury in them."

Isaiah 27:4 — "Fury is not in me: who would set the briers and thorns against me in battle? I would go through them, I would burn them together."

Daniel 3:19 — "Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury, and the form of his visage was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: therefore he spake, and commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated."

Modern Corruption

God's fury is now widely treated as an embarrassment to be explained away as ancient projection, while men's fury is excused as authenticity — an exact reversal of Scripture's judgment on both.

expand to see more

The modern instinct is to apologize for the wrath of God, treating passages like Ezekiel 5:13 as a primitive people's projection of their own violence onto heaven. The texts resist that handling. God's fury in Scripture is never impulsive, never disproportionate, and never uninformed; it is announced in advance, its cause is named, its remedy is offered, and it accomplishes a stated purpose so that men “shall know that I the LORD have spoken it”. Remove it and nothing better is left in its place: a God with no settled heat against evil is a God indifferent to the wronged, and the cross becomes an extravagance answering no real necessity.

At the same time the age has grown tender toward human fury, which it renames passion or authenticity and treats as evidence of sincerity. Daniel 3:19 gives the biblical portrait instead: Nebuchadnezzar's fury changed the form of his visage and drove him to heat a furnace sevenfold, which accomplished precisely nothing except the deaths of his own men. Scripture's counsel is consistent — the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God, and he that is slow to anger is better than the mighty. Recover both halves: fear the fury of God, which is just; distrust your own, which disfigures.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chemah (heat, rage, fury) is the burning-heat word used of both God and men; 'aph (nostril, anger) and Greek thumos (passionate heat) fill out the field.

expand to see more

Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, burning anger, fury; the word in Jeremiah 4:4 and Ezekiel 5:13.

Hebrew 'aph (H639) — nostril, face, anger; the physical image behind the biblical language of wrath.

Hebrew qin'ah (H7068) — zeal, jealousy; the disposition Ezekiel names as the ground of the LORD's speaking.

Aramaic chema (H2528) — fury, rage; the word describing Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 3:19.

Greek thumos (G2372) — passion, heat of anger; distinguished from orge, settled wrath, in the New Testament.

Usage

"“Lest my fury come forth like fire” — divine fury is announced beforehand and may be turned aside."

"“Fury is not in me” — the LORD can truly deny fury toward His own vineyard."

"“Full of fury, and the form of his visage was changed” — human fury disfigures and unseats reason."
